newsitem.title: USA: Warmer, dry weather expected in U.S. Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Warmer, dry weather expected in U.S. Midwest.

text.p: U.S. Midwest farmers should be able to harvest corn and soybeans this week as drier weather settles over the region and temperatures warm to near normal, several meteorologists said.

"The Midwest will be in a drier than normal pattern during the first half of October," said Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis in his daily report. "The only shower system of note during the next seven days will be associated with a cold front which will sweep from northwest to southeast across the belt Wednesday and Thursday."
Over the weekend, the eastern corn belt saw rainfall amounts mostly below 0.10 inch with general coverage.

There were reports of below freezing temperatures Monday morning in Flint and Lansing, Michigan, said Weather Services Corp's Joel Burgio. The normal freeze date for Lansing is Oct 8 and for Flint it is Oct 12, he said.
This week, temperatures were expected to be warm until Wednesday with no precipitation, Burgio said.
"It starts to cool of Wednesday," he said. "It doesn't appear that we will have a hard freeze."
Low temperatures during that time should be in the 30s Farenheit in extreme northern portions of the belt with 40s and 50s F elsewhere, he said.
There was a chance of scattered to widely scattered showers in the western corn belt on Wednesday and the eastern corn belt Thursday, he said.
Long-range forecasts indicated temperatures would be above normal for two days, then normal for one day and below normal for two days, said Weather Express Chief Forecaster Fred Gesser.
"There will be three cold fronts over the next 10 days, none of which looks wet," Gesser said.

He forecast rainfall of 0.10 to 0.25 inch with less than 50 percent coverage. Subfreezing temperatures were possible in the Dakotas, Nebraska, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan but a killing freeze was not likely in the main growing regions.
